 USDA proposes SNAP eligibility overhaul, could cut benefits for millions
 Published:  November 10, 2026 at 7:45 PM Tags:  USDA , SNAP (Nam Y. Huh, Copyright 2025 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.) The U.S. Department of Agriculture is proposing a sweeping change to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program that could remove food assistance from more than 6 million people.
 The proposed rule, published Nov. 10, 2026, would limit automatic SNAP eligibility to only households receiving direct cash assistance under the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program. The public has until Dec. 10, 2026, to submit comments.
 Recommended Videos
 What is categorical eligibility?
 Currently, households can qualify for SNAP automatically — without a separate income or resource review — if all members receive benefits from a state program funded by TANF. That includes not just cash assistance, but also non-cash benefits like childcare referrals or access to an 800-number connecting families to services.
 States have used that flexibility to expand SNAP eligibility well beyond the program’s original income and resource limits — a practice known as broad-based categorical eligibility, or BBCE. As of December 2025, 46 states use BBCE. Of those, 37 states have set gross income limits higher than the federal SNAP threshold of 130% of the Federal Poverty Guidelines, and 41 states have eliminated resource limits entirely.
 Why USDA says the system needs reform
 The USDA says BBCE has drifted far from Congress’ original intent, which was to reduce administrative paperwork — not expand who qualifies for benefits.
 The department points to cases where households with significant financial assets have received SNAP benefits in states with no resource limits — including a widely cited case of a millionaire in Minnesota who received food stamps through a BBCE loophole.
 “It is irresponsible to Congress and the taxpayer to support regulations that permit this practice,” the proposed rule states.
 A 2012 Government Accountability Office report found payment errors in BBCE households at a rate of 17.2%, compared to just 6.7% for other SNAP households. The USDA estimates that 11.5% of participating SNAP households — roughly 2.5 million households containing 5.4 million individuals — currently have resources above the SNAP limit.
 Who would lose benefits?
 The USDA estimates approximately 3.2 million households — containing 6.3 million individuals — would no longer qualify for SNAP once the rule takes full effect in fiscal year 2029.
 The rule would also affect other nutrition programs:
 School meals: About 1.78 million children would lose automatic eligibility for free school meals, though approximately 97% would still qualify through a separate income-based process. An estimated 28,000 children would be required to pay full price. 
 Summer EBT: Approximately 42,000 children could lose Summer Electronic Benefit Transfer benefits starting in summer 2029. 
 WIC: About 5,500 women, infants, and children currently eligible through BBCE would lose WIC eligibility entirely. 
 What it would cost — and save
 The USDA projects the rule would reduce federal SNAP spending by approximately $44.65 billion over five years from fiscal years 2027 through 2031. States would see a net reduction of roughly $5.24 billion in SNAP spending, though administrative costs are expected to increase by approximately $928.5 million as states adjust their eligibility systems.
 The department also estimates more than 840,000 one- and two-person households currently receive the minimum SNAP benefit of $23 per month solely because of BBCE — representing nearly $214 million paid to households exceeding SNAP’s statutory income or resource limits.
 A second attempt at reform
 This is not the first time the federal government has tried to reform categorical eligibility. The Trump administration proposed a similar change in July 2019, which the Biden administration withdrew in June 2021.
 The current proposal ties categorical eligibility specifically to the federal definition of TANF “assistance” — cash, payments, vouchers, and benefits designed to meet a family’s ongoing basic needs — rather than the broader range of non-cash services states have used to confer BBCE. The USDA says this approach is simpler for states to implement than the 2019 framework.
 How to comment
 The public can submit comments through Dec. 10, 2026:
 Online: regulations.gov, docket number FNA-2026-0661 
 Email: sm.fn.snappdbrules@usda.gov 
 Mail: SNAP Program Development Division, Food and Nutrition Administration, 5601 Sunnyside Ave., Beltsville, MD 20705
